Full stack AI features live or die on the contract between the model and your code. Here is a design decision I made on a Python and React.js project that I'd make again.

The project was an expense categoriser and cashflow forecaster for SME finance. Users upload bank CSVs and the app uses an LLM to categorise each transaction.

The first version let the model return free text, then parsed it with regex. It worked on the examples I tried and broke on the first messy description.

The trade-off I chose:

→ Free text: fast to prototype, flexible, fragile in production. Every parser change is a bug risk.
→ Structured outputs: a fixed schema with allowed categories, validated before anything touches PostgreSQL. More upfront work, far fewer silent failures.

My rule now: if the output will be stored, displayed as data or used to make a decision, define the schema first. Use free text only for things a human reads and nothing downstream depends on.

For full stack engineers, this also means the React.js front end and the Python backend agree on the same types, so a model change can't quietly break the UI.

Hiring managers, I'd like to know how you decide between flexible and strict output formats on your AI features. Engineers, what has bitten you most: the model, the parser, or the schema?

The 2027 Agent Builder: A Zero-to-Shipped Roadmap That Starts With One Loop, Not One Framework
#UpSkillRealm

1. The Mental Model & The Prerequisite Foundation
An AI agent consists of four core parts: a language model, a set of tools, a loop, and a stop condition. Beginners fail because they adopt heavy frameworks before understanding the loop underneath.
 * The Six-Week Prerequisite: Skip ML theory and GPUs. Spend six weeks mastering Python basics, HTTP/JSON parsing, environment variables, and reliable API calls with proper error handling.
 * Prompts as Specifications: Treat system prompts as strict job descriptions containing four sections: role, task, constraints, and output schema.

2. Core Engineering Disciplines
 * Hand-Built Loops First: Code a message list, tool registry, dispatcher, and step cap manually. You will immediately encounter malformed arguments, repeated calls, and infinite loops—fix these with deterministic code, not prompt tweaks.
 * Tools as Contracts & MCP: Design atomic, single-job tools with three-sentence descriptions (what it does, when to use it, what it returns), capped output sizes, and actionable error messages. Wrap them in a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server—the baseline interoperability standard for 2027.
 * Three-Layer Memory: Manage working memory (context window), session memory (active scratchpad), and long-term memory (persisted facts). Summarize tool outputs aggressively so agents don't drown in history.
 * Four-Layer Evals: Build 30 test tasks with known outcomes before tuning. Grade tool selection, argument correctness, final answer, and trajectory independently to diagnose failures systematically.
 * Disciplined Multi-Agent Scaling: Only use orchestrator-worker patterns when subtasks are genuinely independent, always benchmarking against a single-agent baseline to justify token overhead.

3. The 2027 Hiring Portfolio
Hiring managers no longer screen for framework buzzwords. Ship three public projects—one hand-built loop, one MCP server, and one evaluated agent with full execution traces—accompanied by write-ups detailing what broke and how you debugged it.

My number this week is 10.1%, and it isn't a hiring number.

It's how much contract staffing in Indian tech grew in FY26, against 2.3% growth in permanent tech employment, per a CIEL HR study reported by the Economic Times on 18 November. Nearly 80% of the sector's hiring demand sits with experienced professionals, the four-to-eight year band the biggest slice. Demand for AI/ML skills rose 86.5% in that study, and for agentic AI engineers 260%. CIEL also projects contract roles at close to a quarter of GCC positions by the end of 2026, a projection rather than a count.

For anyone entering next year: the work is coming back as defined projects and narrow skills, not as permanent entry-level seats. A fresher isn't competing with another fresher so much as with a two-year contractor who knows the stack. The roles that hold are the ones with a named skill attached, data and security and applied AI, while plain engineering hiring stays thin.

From where I sit, finishing a BCA in an AI and ML programme, the eligibility filter costs more interviews than any skill gap. Plenty of these contract roles open with a B.Tech preference before anyone reads what you can do.

If you've been hunting in Indian tech this quarter, did you get more callbacks for permanent roles or for contract ones?

77% of leaders say AI is increasing contractor demand

Upwork research found that 77% of business leaders say the AI era is increasing their need to hire contract workers with specialized skills.

That's not a hiring freeze story.
That's a skills story.

If you're early in your career, the takeaway is uncomfortable but useful:
Generic is getting harder to hire.
Specific is getting easier to pay for.

What "specific" looks like:
→ One tool or platform you know deeply
→ One business problem you can solve end to end
→ One result you can point to

If you manage a team, the takeaway is different:
You may not need fewer people.
You may need a different mix of people, contracted, specialized, and onboarded fast.

Either way, the question isn't "will AI take the job?"
It's "which skills will companies pay a premium for?"

What's the one skill you're doubling down on this year?

India’s two largest IT firms want up to 14,900 forward deployed engineers. About 1,200 people in India are ready for the role today.
 
The plans:

 • TCS: 1–1.5% of its workforce, or 5,900 to 8,900 people (Reuters)
 • Infosys: 6,000 over the next few years
 • Ready supply: about 1,200 (CIEL HR)
 
Two other numbers say more about what happens next:

 • 75–80% of FDE job postings in India are solutions or implementation roles with a new title (Source: UnearthInsight)
 • 47% of enterprises plan to upskill their own engineers, and 31% plan to hire from outside (Source: Scaler-CMR Report)
 
So most of India’s FDEs will be today’s engineers with a course and a new designation.
 
Whether that works depends on the contract. An FDE needs permission to:

 • Sit with the people doing the work
 • Change the systems they use
 • Answer for whether it still runs next week
 
A fixed-scope services contract grants none of this. Put a newly trained FDE back inside one and the work is still implementation.
 
Employers know where the difficulty lies:

 • 51% test FDE candidates with a deployment or troubleshooting case, and 24% with a coding test
 • Production deployment: 77% call it important, 19% can find it
 • Customer engagement: 61% call it important, 25% can find it
 
Neither is mainly an AI skill. Engineers learn both by owning a system at a customer when it fails. Training can rehearse that. It can’t hand anyone the pager.
 
The squeeze lands on software companies. Close to 80% of FDE hiring is in Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Hyderabad, at ₹70–90 lakh a year for experienced people. A platform vendor hiring one FDE now bids against TCS and Infosys, and the role stays open another quarter.

At KnackLabs, forward deployed engineering has been in our DNA since 2016: our engineers sit with the customer’s team from discovery to production, and answer for what runs after launch.

One question sorts the market: when the system fails at the customer at 2 am, whose phone rings?
 
If it’s a ticket queue, the engineer was never forward deployed.

I opened my calendar to help people navigating layoffs. I ended up learning a lot myself.

Two days ago, I opened my calendar for 1:1 conversations with people affected by layoffs or struggling to find their next opportunity.

The response completely surprised me.

Here's what happened in the last 48 hours:

- 744 page views and 310 unique visitors on my topmate.io page
- 32 sessions booked
- 33,500+ impressions on that single LinkedIn post
- Nearly 50,000 impressions across the week

More importantly, I spent hours speaking with mobile developers, backend engineers, QA specialists, and ERP architects with 2 to 12+ years of experience.

Different backgrounds. Different experiences. But surprisingly similar challenges.

Here are 4 patterns I noticed:

Applications without responses: Sending 60 to 70+ applications through job portals and barely hearing back.

Lengthy hiring processes: Going through 5 to 6 interview rounds, only to face delayed decisions or no updates.

Changing market expectations: Experienced engineers facing rejections as companies restructure teams, reconsider budgets, and adapt to AI.

Limited visibility: Depending entirely on traditional job portals instead of building a visible professional presence.

Here are some things we explored during these conversations:

1. Alternative earning opportunities

Exploring global AI training and contract platforms where engineers and language experts can find project-based work, with some opportunities offering $10 to $40/hour.

2. Proof of work over resumes

Creating short demo videos of real projects, sharing technical learnings, and demonstrating skills publicly instead of waiting for a resume to get shortlisted.

3. Community over cold applications

Connecting with local tech communities, developer conferences, meetups, and peer networks where meaningful conversations and referrals can happen.

4. Building instead of waiting

Using this transition period to build small products, experiment with AI workflows, and explore freelance consulting.

These are not guaranteed shortcuts to a job. They are additional ways to create opportunities while continuing the job search.

One more honest learning:

Around 10 to 15% of the people who booked a free session didn't show up or even send a message.

I completely understand that circumstances can change. But every unused slot could have gone to someone else who genuinely needed that conversation.

So, going forward, I'm introducing a small ₹149 commitment fee for each 30-minute 1:1 session.

This isn't about monetizing someone's difficult situation. It's simply to reduce no-shows and ensure that every available slot goes to someone who is ready to show up and make the most of our conversation.

If you're navigating a layoff, struggling with your job search, or simply want to brainstorm your next career move, let's connect.

HRBP in the IT Sector: Is Your Business Scaling Faster Than Your People Systems?

Growing an IT company from 10 to 250 employees is not just about winning more projects, hiring developers and expanding technical capabilities.

At some point, the challenges that affect business growth are no longer purely technical. They become people and organisational challenges.

Consider a few situations:
1. Your project pipeline is growing, but are your skills keeping pace?
You may have developers on your payroll, yet struggle to find the right capabilities for an upcoming project. Hiring externally becomes the immediate solution, while existing employee skills and internal mobility remain underutilised.

2. Your best developers are becoming managers. But are they equipped to lead people?
Technical expertise doesn't automatically translate into people-management capability. Without structured support, managers can struggle with performance conversations, team conflicts, employee motivation and accountability.

3. You are hiring to meet demand, but what happens when project requirements change?
Are you forecasting workforce requirements against your actual project pipeline? Could better resource allocation, skills mapping and cross-training reduce unnecessary hiring and unproductive capacity?

4. Your attrition numbers look manageable, but are you losing the right people?
Losing one critical architect, project lead or experienced developer can have a disproportionate impact on delivery continuity, client relationships and team performance.
Are you measuring attrition only as a percentage, or understanding its impact on business operations?

5. You have introduced performance appraisals, but do they measure business contribution?
Are employees evaluated against meaningful delivery outcomes, quality, collaboration, innovation and role-specific expectations, or primarily through task completion and subjective manager feedback?

6. Your organisation is adopting AI, but is your workforce evolving with it?
Are job responsibilities changing? Are employees being reskilled? Are managers prepared to lead teams where human capabilities and AI-enabled productivity work together?

These are not isolated HR problems. They are business challenges with people at their centre.

What can a Strategic HR Business Partner bring to a growing IT business?

Skills-based workforce planning aligned with project demand.
Resource utilisation and internal talent deployment strategies.
Technical manager development and leadership coaching.
Performance frameworks linked to delivery and business outcomes.
Critical talent retention and career progression.
People analytics that help leadership anticipate workforce risks.
AI-related workforce transformation and change management.

The objective is not to introduce more HR processes or technology for the sake of it.
It is to help business leaders make better workforce decisions, strengthen management capability and build an organisation that can scale without creating unnecessary operational complexity.

For IT founders and CEOs leading teams of 10–250 employees:

Are your current people systems equipped for the next stage of your business growth?

I would be interested in exchanging perspectives with technology business leaders on where people strategy can make a measurable difference.

If you are exploring strategic HRBP support on a contract or part-time basis, I would welcome a conversation.

so he switched on an AI to handle them and went back to hiring.

"still waiting on that contract. 50% off year one, as agreed."

he opened linkedin and scrolled up.

--

most of what the AI had sent was fine. a few were good.
then he got to her thread.

she'd pushed back on price. the AI, trying to be helpful:

"i hear you. i could probably do 50% off for the first year
if we get started this month."

he'd never offered that to anyone.

"deal. send the contract."

"amazing! contract coming your way."

that was a tuesday afternoon. he'd been in an interview.
his price for her was $120,000 a year.

--

he honoured it. $60,000 gone, in his name, in writing.
he felt he had to.

then it got worse.
she's in a peer group with two of his customers.
both asked about "the first-year price" at their renewals.

he'd been talking to buyers for nine days
and hadn't heard a word of it.

it can only use what the company wrote down.

read the drafts. see for yourself.

if you're about to let AI reply for you, ask the vendor one thing.

My AI curriculum passed every fact check. That's what made it dangerous.

Write down what each module assumes you already have. Then check whether the AI filled the gap. It will, and it won't tell you when it started guessing.

I rebuilt a Harvard Data Science Review outline into a free 14-day AI governance plan with Claude, then audited it like anyone else's work.
The facts held up. 23 of 23 links resolved. 6 of 6 regulatory claims correct — the EU AI Act deferral, Colorado's replacement law, NIST's framework, ISO 42001, NYC's bias-audit law, NIST's generative AI profile. 6 of 6 readings correctly named and dated.

"AI makes things up" was not the failure. The document has a seam, and the seam is where the links stop.

Every fact is sourced. Every task is not. 11 of 14 days tell me to work on "my organization" — footprint map, shadow AI inventory, stakeholder grid, board memo.
Could I have researched that from public information? Partly. Filings, regulator findings, published audits. That gets you which vendors are named and what a regulator found.
It doesn't get you what tools staff actually use, what's in the contracts, who holds the budget, what the data pipeline looks like. Public research stops there.
That's where the model doesn't stop.

It keeps writing. Same voice, same confidence. The Colorado date is real. The stakeholder grid is plausible. Both are sentences in the same font.

By day three the learner has stopped looking, because 23 links worked and nothing had been wrong yet. That's what the accuracy buys. Trust — which the unsourced half then spends.
I tested it. Asked an AI to play the organization. It answered fluently, in detail, about a company that doesn't exist.

Everything else I checked instead of filling. Retyped the outline by hand and got a 404 from a link that was never broken. Swapped in a real case — NYC's audit of 32 hiring-tool vendors. Worked for one day. Re-checked every date and found a tool that returns 200, looks live, and has been unmaintained for years.
Then I asked the same model that wrote the curriculum to audit it. One unchecked claim checking another.

The audit only worked when it stopped being a conversation. 23 HTTP requests. Six titles matched against arXiv. A statute checked against Colorado's own site. Facts you can verify outside the model are the only facts it can't fill in for you.

So the sin isn't that a student would make something up. It's that they wouldn't have to. The writing does it, in the same voice as everything that was true.

Auditing your AI is the one step that isn't self-referential. It's the only way to find the seam.
What does this task assume I have? An organization. A dataset. A licence. A colleague. A paid account. Name it — or you'll never notice the model named it for you.

Where does your AI stop knowing and start sounding like it knows?

A $300,000 industrial order can strengthen the sales forecast and still leave next month’s payroll short.

The author’s AI finance toolkit connects pricing, cash and hiring for growing B2B companies. I’d start with one decision: can we add a permanent sales role before the orders in our pipeline turn into cash?

Consider a hypothetical $300,000 order with a 25% contribution margin. If the customer pays 60 days after delivery and the supplier requires a $90,000 deposit at order placement, the $75,000 contribution comes with an immediate cash outflow. The timing matters even if the order is signed and the margin holds.

I’d have Sales and Finance review the largest CRM opportunities together. Sales would verify the buyer’s technical approval, purchase order status and delivery date. Finance would map supplier deposits, payroll and expected collections into a rolling 13-week cash forecast. I’d use AI to flag missing terms and draft a downside scenario. The team would verify those assumptions against quotes, contracts and payment history.

Each week, I’d track the contribution margin of won orders after commissions and variable service costs, plus the lowest projected cash balance over the next 13 weeks. I’d approve the hire if the margin supports the added payroll and cash stays above our agreed buffer even if a major order slips or a customer pays late. If the buffer is breached, I’d test a customer deposit or milestone billing and rerun the forecast before committing.

The supply chain trends report for 2026 makes one thing clear: procurement is moving from a cost-center function to a strategic intelligence driver, and SAP MM sits at the center of that shift. But the conversation I am having with hiring managers and teams is not about new features—it is about how to prepare for the architectural demands that 2026 will impose on MM landscapes.

The most under-discussed challenge right now is the intersection of SAP MM with agentic AI and orchestration. We are seeing the first wave of AI agents that can autonomously negotiate with suppliers, reorder based on predictive demand, or flag contract compliance risks before invoices hit. The problem is that most MM implementations today are not designed to feed clean, structured data into these agents. They are built on transactional workflows optimized for manual intervention, not machine consumption.

For recruiters: I am seeing a gap between candidates who know MM transactional processes and those who understand how to architect MM data models for AI consumption. The latter is what every forward-thinking supply chain team will need by Q3 2026. If you are screening for MM roles, look for someone who can talk about how they structured material master data or inventory valuation to support real-time analytics and autonomous decision-making, not just how they configured a purchase order workflow.

The February 2026 SAP MM certification updates are also revealing a shift. The syllabus now includes substantial content on sustainability tracking, carbon footprint integration at the material level, and supplier collaboration in the cloud. This is not optional anymore. Companies that ignore these dimensions in their MM design will face regulatory friction and audit risks within 18 months.

What separates a good MM consultant from a great one in 2026 is the ability to design processes that are both standardized for cloud compliance and flexible enough to absorb AI-driven recommendations. The clean-core mandate is not just about technical architecture; it is about rethinking every MM transaction as a data point for a smarter system.

The question I keep asking myself: are we building MM processes that enable AI, or are we building AI that compensates for broken MM processes? That distinction will define the next generation of supply chain leaders.

• New business openings and tenant expansion
• Sustained customer spending

A VP of data science and a Chief Data Officer do different jobs, but most searches treat them alike.

In Axial Search's analysis of director, VP and C-suite Data Science postings in the US and Canada, 78% of VP roles mention a programming language such as Python, SQL, Java or Scala. For C-suite roles the share is 24%.

The VP is still expected to build. That means reviewing code, guiding technical choices and staying close to the work.

The Chief Data Officer is judged on something else: strategy, governance and leading change across the business.

A recruiter who sends over resumes with the right titles will miss that gap. The brief and the assessment have to change with the level, and a firm running C-suite searches should be able to show how.

The same logic applies one step earlier. Staffing firms fill contract and volume roles, agencies place permanent hires, and executive search firms run a defined search for a leader. Pick the type before you pick the firm.

Then check AI coverage. If the role is moving toward AI, you want a recruiter who can staff the role you are heading toward, not only the one you have today.

This is for executives hiring a director, VP or Chief Data Officer, and for hiring managers choosing who to run the search. Axial Search has written up how six data science recruiters compare on focus, AI coverage and levels.

A search brief that reads the same for a VP and a Chief Data Officer is probably testing the wrong things for one of them.

And concluding with NEUDC recap part 3:  

Firms
  
Mohit Karnani: Cash transfers disbursed throuh a novel digital wallet with restricted redemption (at local retailers) in Chile do lead to increased prices on the part of participating firms (the redemption locations), but this is attenuated in retailers facing more competitive markets.
  
Shreya Chandra: Incentives for on-time arrival in garment manufacturing in India lead to increased production and earnings (especially for female workers), and increases in output and revenue at the firm level.
  
Leonardo Peñaloza-Pacheco: Large-scale migration (from Venezuela) into Colombia increases productivity but did not raise wages as firms increased their wage markdowns (as self-employment became a less valuable outside option).
  
Daniel Overbeck: Delays in receiving VAT refunds in Zambia have a range of negative effects on firms (reducing firms' sales, profits, investment, and employment) - consistent with binding liquidity constraints.
 
Markus Poschke: Cross-country variation in skill endowment predicts much of the cross-country variation in the firm size distribution.
  
Alix Naugler: A threshold-based (size-based) formalization policy in Vietnam leads to selective formalization (in which informality is restructured) rather than eliminating informality.
  
Jonah Rexer: Weak institutions can generate advantages for local firms (vis-a-vis multinational firms); in weak institutional environments, local takeovers of mining firms increases output.
  
Labor
  
Anna Vitali: Firms in Uganda face substantial and hard-to-predict labor demand with very high adjustment costs, and generally low labor utilization.
  
Jimena Rico-Straffon: Piped water shortages reduce formal labor supply in Mexico City, though informal employees increase hours.
  
David Qihang Wu: High rates of separation among workers in industrial parks in Ethiopia seem to reflect low productivity, not better outside options.
  
Juan Felipe Ladino Mateus: Adoption of digitized methods of public hiring in Colombia reduces political disretion in bureaucrat hiring.
  
Palak Suri: Among police officers in India, women value proximity to home, better infrastructure, flexibility + safety more than men.
  
Neha Betai: Onset of generative AI leads to sharp declines in outsourcing to devleoping countries, with fewer tasks and contracts, but more complex and higher-valued tasks for those who remain in the sector.

Most HR automation demos show the happy path. This one shows what happens when a CV is unreadable, a policy answer has no evidence, a certificate is requested twice, or a service goes down mid-run.

I built Smart HR Operations Hub from zero: 10 n8n workflows, 282 nodes, and a rulebook that decides what the AI is and is not allowed to do.

What the system does

→ A router validates a shared request envelope, classifies it, and dispatches across six webhook routes. Low confidence goes to a supervisor agent. It can recommend a route, never an outcome.

→ CV intake extracts fields from text PDFs and falls back to vision OCR for scans. Empty fields stay empty. A stable email|job_id key stops duplicate applications.

→ Recruitment compares the CV with the job using cited evidence — but an allowlisted HR reviewer, not the model, moves a candidate to Hired.

→ Onboarding creates one employee record and reads uploaded documents. A blurry ID becomes "Needs Review"; OCR never authenticates an identity.

→ The policy assistant retrieves only active policy chunks with BM25. If citations do not verify, it abstains and refers the question to HR.

→ A certificate passes five gates — employee exists, policy evidence present, allowlisted HR Manager, explicit "approve", not already issued — before exactly one PDF is created.

Why it matters

HR workflows touch jobs, identity documents and pay-adjacent decisions. A fast answer that invents a fact is worse than a slow answer that says "I don't know". So every agent output is checked by a deterministic node, every restricted decision needs a human, every run writes an audit row, and stable keys make retries safe. That is the difference between a demo that impresses and a system you could defend.

The numbers

• 10 workflows / 282 nodes on n8n Cloud
• 6+ AI agent roles, each with a written contract
• 3 human authorization gates: hiring, leave exceptions, certificate release
• 9-sheet datastore, 34 active policy chunks, 6 router webhook routes
• 18/18 tests · 282/282 nodes linted · 93/93 package checks
• Retry and catch-up proven on live executions 543, 546 and 548

The part I am proudest of is not the architecture. It is the 30-problem log: a webhook returning 500 because I edited an active workflow, reads multiplying 4×7×3×6×39 rows, two catch-up rows from a five-second test gap, and an expired trial that forced a rebuild with new IDs. Every failure has a root cause and a fix, in writing.

All data is fictional. No real personal data, no credentials in exports, nothing uploaded to a public repo.

Swipe through all 10 workflows — from the router to the retry target.

For a long time, the ATS has been a system of record for the employer. The candidate was someone the system tracked.
 
That’s changing. Providers building toward candidate-experience-first are using this wave of AI to do what the old ATS never did. They give the candidate a persistent profile, run AI across the whole hiring workflow instead of one screening step, and let signal move both ways between employer and candidate. They still deliver the outcomes the employer requires.
 
That combination is creating new platform gravity. Presence, brand, and first-party candidate data compound until a provider becomes the default reference point in its category, because switching away costs more than staying.
 
If you lead talent acquisition or buy TA technology, the space you’re evaluating is reorganizing around this. Your next ATS contract may be buying where the market has been, not where it’s headed.
 
I mapped it in my report, The ATS Is Splitting. The next report is almost here, and it builds on this one.
